headline: A 1940s Oklahoma Occultist's Verse Circulates Online as Ancient Wisdom
lede: The passage shared here — on karma, the creative power of thought, and alignment with cosmic law — is attributed to *The Emerald Tablets of Thoth the Atlantean*, a text widely presented online as ancient Hermetic scripture. It is not ancient. It was composed by a mid-20th-century American occultist who claimed, in shifting accounts, to have discovered it in the Great Pyramid of Giza, received it from Atlantean emissaries, and channeled it by telepathy.
body:
The passage is from *The Emerald Tablets of Thoth the Atlantean* — a work widely circulated online as ancient Hermetic scripture. It is not ancient. It was composed by Maurice Doreal, born Claude Dodgin in pre-statehood Oklahoma in 1902, who claimed to have translated it from physical tablets he found inside the Great Pyramid of Giza in 1925. His story changed over the years: later versions held that Atlantean emissaries escorted him to a cave beneath Mount Shasta, or that the transmission arrived by telepathy. Around 1930, Doreal founded the **Brotherhood of the White Temple** in Denver, built a correspondence-course business in occult cosmology, and eventually relocated his congregation to a walled compound in Sedalia, Colorado, in 1953 ahead of a predicted nuclear apocalypse. Researcher Jason Colavito has documented specific borrowings in the tablets from H.P. Lovecraft, Frank Belknap Long's *The Hounds of Tindalos* (1929), and Robert E. Howard's "The Shadow Kingdom" (*Weird Tales*, August 1929), placing the composition firmly in the late 1930s or early 1940s.

The name is a deliberate echo of a genuine historical object. The actual *Emerald Tablet* — singular — attributed to *Hermes Trismegistus*, the syncretic Greco-Egyptian figure merging the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian Thoth, is a cryptic alchemical text roughly a paragraph long, preserved in Arabic manuscripts from the 8th or 9th century CE. Its most famous line — "as above, so below" — shaped centuries of alchemical speculation and prompted a translation by Isaac Newton. That text bears no relationship to Doreal's multi-chapter verse beyond the shared borrowed name; the confusion, endemic online, is partly by design.

The philosophical content of the quoted passage has genuine antecedents — they just do not begin with Doreal. The ideas of thought as creative force and cause-and-effect as cosmic law run through *Hermeticism*, Stoic philosophy, and *Neoplatonism*. Their more immediate ancestor is *The Kybalion*, an influential 1908 *New Thought* text attributed to "Three Initiates" (almost certainly the prolific Chicago occultist William Walker Atkinson), which codified a *Principle of Mentalism* — "The All is Mind; the Universe is Mental" — and a Principle of Cause and Effect in language nearly identical to Doreal's verse. *New Thought*, the American metaphysical movement from which both texts descend, holds that mental states directly shape material circumstances; William James called it "a genuine religious power" in *The Varieties of Religious Experience* (1902).

On social media, Doreal's verses now circulate stripped of attribution, labeled simply "ancient Hermetic wisdom." Their karma-and-manifestation themes slot naturally into the *Law of Attraction* ecosystem — the contemporary heir of New Thought — which generates hundreds of millions of views on TikTok and Instagram. The text's other legacy is less benign: David Icke drew directly from Doreal's writings about underground serpent-people in human form when constructing his reptilian conspiracy theory in the 1990s, a reminder of how comfortably pseudo-ancient scripture migrates between spiritual self-help and paranoid fantasy.

concepts.definition: A philosophical and spiritual tradition based on texts attributed to Hermes Trismegistus, a syncretic figure combining the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian god Thoth. The core texts — the Corpus Hermeticum — were written in Egypt in the 2nd–3rd centuries CE and rediscovered by Western Europe in the 15th century. They concern cosmology, alchemy, and spiritual transformation; scholars date them to late antiquity, not ancient Egypt.

A legendary figure combining the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian god Thoth, credited in late-antique and medieval tradition with authoring foundational texts of alchemy, astrology, and magic. The name means "Hermes the Thrice-Great." Modern scholarship treats the texts attributed to him as composed in the 2nd–3rd centuries CE by unknown authors in Greco-Roman Egypt, not by an ancient divine scribe.

An American religious and metaphysical movement originating in the 1830s, most associated with healer Phineas Quimby, holding that the mind directly shapes physical reality. Belief, visualization, and positive mental states are said to produce health, abundance, and desired outcomes. Its institutional heirs include the Unity Church and Religious Science; its popular heir is the Law of Attraction.

The New Thought doctrine that thoughts and emotions magnetically attract corresponding material circumstances — dwell on abundance and abundance follows; focus on lack and lack manifests. The phrase reached mass-market audiences through Rhonda Byrne's 2006 book *The Secret*. It has no scientific basis.

A philosophical tradition originating with Plotinus in the 3rd century CE, holding that all existence emanates from a single transcendent source ("the One") through successive levels of reality — intellect, soul, matter. It was a major influence on early Christian theology, Islamic philosophy, Renaissance esotericism, and later occult traditions including the Hermetic texts.

One of the "Seven Hermetic Principles" codified in The Kybalion (1908): "The All is Mind; the Universe is Mental." It holds that consciousness is the fundamental substrate of reality and that thoughts therefore shape material outcomes. The principle is New Thought doctrine dressed in Hermetic vocabulary, not a direct transmission of ancient teaching.

An occult religious organization founded by Maurice Doreal in Denver around 1930. It operated through correspondence courses selling Doreal's teachings on Atlantis, cosmic law, and hidden history. In 1953, anticipating nuclear apocalypse, Doreal relocated the group to a walled compound in Sedalia, Colorado. The organization still exists and sells Doreal's works online.

The practice of falsely attributing a text to a famous, ancient, or divinely inspired author in order to lend it authority. The real author writes under an invented ancient name. Doreal's Thoth attribution is a modern example; religious history contains many others, from the deutero-Pauline letters to the ancient Hermetic dialogues themselves.

books.title: The Emerald Tablets of Thoth the Atlantean
books.author: Maurice Doreal
books.summary: Fifteen verse chapters composed by the American occultist Maurice Doreal (born Claude Dodgin, 1902–1963), falsely presented as a translation of pre-Flood tablets discovered in the Great Pyramid of Giza. Researchers have identified borrowings from 1920s–30s pulp science fiction including Lovecraft and Robert E. Howard. Despite scholarly consensus that the work is a modern pseudepigraphical composition, it circulates widely online as ancient Hermetic wisdom, most often without attribution to Doreal.

books.title: The Kybalion: A Study of the Hermetic Philosophy of Ancient Egypt and Greece
books.author: Three Initiates (attributed; almost certainly William Walker Atkinson)
books.summary: An influential 1908 occult text that codified "Seven Hermetic Principles" — including the Principle of Mentalism and the Principle of Cause and Effect — in accessible language for American New Thought audiences. Scholars classify it as New Thought doctrine retrofitted onto Hermetic vocabulary rather than a genuine transmission of ancient teaching. It is the closest intellectual ancestor to the philosophy expressed in Doreal's tablets, sharing nearly identical formulations.

fact_check: The passage is presented as ancient Hermetic scripture. It is not. It was composed by the American occultist Maurice Doreal in the late 1930s or early 1940s and first circulated by his Brotherhood of the White Temple in mimeographed form. Doreal offered at least three mutually contradictory accounts of its origin; none is supported by independent evidence. The text is frequently confused online with the genuine ancient Emerald Tablet of Hermes Trismegistus — an 8th-to-9th-century Arabic alchemical work, roughly a paragraph long, to which Doreal's multi-chapter composition bears no textual relationship. The shared name and Thoth attribution are Doreal's invention.
